node-1.label: Patient presented with weakness, bloating, anorexia, decreased urine output for 10 days, and fever with low back pain

node-2.label: 53-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B virus infection (>30 years), denied history of infectious diseases (typhoid, tuberculosis), chronic diseases (hypertension, diabetes), and recent surgery or trauma

node-3.label: Physical examination on admission showed blood pressure 153/89 mmHg

node-4.label: On July 15, patient developed fever (39°C) with obvious tenderness of the left lumbar vertebra; on July 16, temperature increased to 40.2°C accompanied by chills, severe low back pain, and forced position

why.why: New expert analyses from Laboratory Medicine and Radiology both conclude that blood culture evidence (TCBS-green colonies, 16S rRNA confirmation, multi-antibiotic sensitivity) confirms definitive bacteremia and is consistent with pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis. The newly noted grayish-white colonies on blood agar and known cirrhosis/ascites add supportive context for an invasive bacterial process. However, no spinal MRI/CT and missing CRP/ESR, urinalysis, and renal function tests still prevent site confirmation, so confidence is adjusted to 0.8.

New expert analyses explicitly state that severe localized vertebral tenderness and forced position favor spinal infection and that renal infection is less likely. The new evidence of cirrhosis/ascites does not explain the localized vertebral findings, and no renal imaging or urinalysis is available. Confidence is reduced to 0.2.

The new expert analyses focus on confirmed Vibrio bacteremia and pyogenic spinal infection; known cirrhosis/ascites may reflect chronic liver disease but does not explain the acute febrile low back pain syndrome. There is still no liver imaging or tumor marker evidence for HCC, so confidence remains low at 0.05.

node-8.label: Blood culture grew organisms on TCBS agar

node-9.label: 16S rRNA sequencing confirmed the pathogen from blood culture

node-10.label: The isolated pathogen is sensitive to multiple antibiotics

node-13.label: Pyogenic spinal infection (vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis) due to antibiotic-sensitive bacteremia

why.why: Expert consensus from Laboratory Medicine and Radiology supports pyogenic spinal infection due to antibiotic-sensitive bacteremia, with definite Vibrio bacteremia on blood culture (TCBS-green, 16S rRNA, multi-antibiotic sensitivity). The newly noted grayish-white blood agar colonies are consistent with gram-negative bacteremia, and cirrhosis/ascites supports an invasive infection. No spinal imaging or inflammatory markers prevent higher confidence, so 0.75.

node-15.label: CRP/ESR, urinalysis, and renal function tests are missing/not reported

why.why: The Laboratory Physician now states Vibrio bacteremia is definite, based on blood culture growing grayish-white on blood agar and green on TCBS, with 16S rRNA confirmation and multi-antibiotic sensitivity. This new explicit expert certainty, plus the new evidence of grayish-white colonies and known cirrhosis/ascites (a predisposing condition), raises confidence to 0.8; species-level confirmation and exposure history are still absent.

node-17.label: Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis due to Vibrio species bacteremia

why.why: New expert analyses support Vibrio bacteremia as definite and note that fever, chills, and severe lumbar tenderness suggest pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis. The newly added cirrhosis/ascites may predispose to invasive Vibrio infection. However, no spinal MRI/CT is available, so the vertebral site remains unconfirmed and confidence is adjusted to 0.7.

node-18.label: Pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis/discitis due to other antibiotic-sensitive bacteria

why.why: Expert analyses strengthen the conclusion that the bloodstream pathogen is Vibrio species by TCBS-green colonies and 16S rRNA. This makes other antibiotic-sensitive bacteria a less likely cause of pyogenic spinal infection. Without species-level confirmation some uncertainty remains, so confidence is reduced to 0.15.

New expert analyses do not provide tuberculosis testing, spinal imaging, or any findings suggesting granulomatous infection. The acute high fever/chills and confirmed Vibrio bacteremia further argue against Pott disease, so confidence remains 0.05.

node-20.label: Spinal epidural abscess secondary to pyogenic vertebral infection

why.why: New expert analyses still lack spinal MRI/CT, so epidural abscess cannot be confirmed. The severe localized vertebral tenderness and forced position keep it a recognized complication of pyogenic vertebral infection, but no new evidence increases its probability; confidence remains 0.1.
